items.content:
In 1994, software was dead. People told me programming was for nerds and that I should become a doctor or a lawyer instead.

In 2004, software was dead. People told me that someone from India would take my job for $5/hour.

In 2014, software was dead. People told me that no-code was going to kill every job and doom my career.

In 2024, software was dead with Devin, Windsurf, Copilot, and OpenAI o1.

We kill software every 10 years, and yet the demand for good Software Engineers has never been higher.

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: For the first time, AI-designed viruses were given to a human patient to fight ...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: For the first time, AI-designed viruses were given to a human patient to fight a drug-resistant infection.

• The viruses are bacteriophages, which only infect bacteria, designed by Omnii-1, a genome language model from Radical Numerics, a startup founded by members of the Arc Institute's Evo team
• The patient's E. coli infection resisted antibiotics and every available phage
• Omnii-1 redesigned the "legs" phages use to grab bacteria, and a cocktail of the new variants wiped out the patient's bacteria in a lab dish
• The cocktail then went to the patient under compassionate use, but the outcome hasn't been shared, citing privacy
• Antibiotic resistance could cause nearly 40M deaths by 2050, and finding the right phage by hand can take months

@theojaffee: "A virus is barely alive. You can just think of them as sort of tiny self-replicators. It literally repurposes the internal machinery of the bacterial cell to make more of itself, and it manufactures so many viruses, the cell will burst, which kills the bacteria."
items.author: @MTSlive
items.summary: Detailed explainer of the first compassionate-use treatment of a patient with AI-designed bacteriophages: Omnii-1, a genome language model from Radical Numerics (Arc Institute Evo alumni), redesigned phage tail proteins to attack a drug-resistant E. coli infection.

items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: OpenAI's former research chief Bob McGrew just raised $232 million to bring AI to American factories.

• The round values Arda at $1.5B, combining a $160M Series A co-led by Altimeter, Accel, and Khosla with a $72M seed
• It's Claude Code or Cursor for manufacturing engineers: an AI agent that turns a product's CAD files into an assembly plan and station layout
• Retraining a human for a design change takes a day, but updating factory automation takes 3 to 6 months
• At Anduril, its first customer, basic work instructions went from 10 hours to 15 minutes
• Next, Arda wants robots to carry out its assembly plans, as the US pushes to bring manufacturing home

@theojaffee: "Manufacturing is a very physical process. It’s very human-intensive. It’s hard to automate in the way that you can automate things that are fully software. But Bob McGrew thinks that we can do it."

items.title: Just watched the @netflix Instadocs about the @OpenAI cyberattack on @huggingface. Super disappointi...
items.content:
Just watched the @netflix Instadocs about the @OpenAI cyberattack on @huggingface. Super disappointing, as they went for maximum anthropomorphism of the technology and full doomer mode.

I spent more than two hours with them trying to correct all their mistakes and ground this in reality, explaining that agents are technological systems, not aliens. But it looks like the drive to scare people for maximum views was too strong.

Also, they didn’t mention the lack of containment and monitoring of the agents, how closed-model safeguards blocked our defensive work, or how we defended ourselves with AI using an open model. And that we still lack a lot of information and transparency, including full agent traces and that companies need to remain accountable for what their agents do.

It ends up being a fun sci-fi movie though!

items.title: The article addresses a fundamental question in training LLMs: when a model is fine-tuned on example...
items.content:
The article addresses a fundamental question in training LLMs: when a model is fine-tuned on examples of good answers (the stage commonly called supervised fine-tuning), how well can it learn to answer new questions, given that most questions have many equally valid answers? Today's standard method minimizes the log-loss, which effectively tries to imitate the exact style and distribution of the human demonstrator. The authors argue this is the wrong target: success should be measured by producing any single good answer, not by cloning the demonstrator's particular way of answering. Math problems, coding tasks, and essay prompts all admit vast numbers of correct responses, so distribution-matching is unnecessarily strict—and, as the article shows, theoretically untenable under the natural modeling assumption.

The article formalizes the task as imitation learning in contextual bandits (one-shot question–answer settings, with no observed rewards at training time) and compares two modeling assumptions. The traditional assumption is that the demonstrator's behavior belongs to a small class of policies. The authors instead assume only that the underlying reward function—which defines which answers are correct—belongs to a small class, and they prove this is a strictly weaker assumption when the demonstrator is optimal. The approach is theoretical: they construct counterexamples showing that the standard maximum-likelihood approach can fail catastrophically under the reward-class assumption (its error can remain arbitrarily close to total failure regardless of how much training data is available), and they design and analyze an alternative algorithm using online-learning tools such as multiplicative weight updates.

one line of questioning we went d...
items.content:
had a lot of fun talking with @HarryStebbings about all things ai

one line of questioning we went done - vertical vs horizontal agents, and how to build them

im bullish on vertical agents, and i think you can create differentiation (from horizontal agents) in three ways:

1/ context: prompts, skills, tools - all of this is specific to your domain, pretty easy to provide, and gives domain specific context to the agent

2/ harness: harder to tweak than context, but can alter fundemental behavior of the agent

3/ model: hardest to tweak of all, but obviously changes behavior greatly

i think most agent engineers these days are still tweaking 1 and 2 (in that order)

nb: regardless of what layer you tweak at, as the base models change you should revisit your context/harness/model every 3-6 months (and generally remove cruft that is no longer needed)

https://t.co/gmA8oyfxiX

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Sam Altman's 3 endgames for AI include one where a single lab melts everyone el...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Sam Altman's 3 endgames for AI include one where a single lab melts everyone else's GPUs.

• The other 2 options are an IAEA-style watchdog that inspects labs, or a CERN-style merger of the labs dubbed the "Demis plan"
• An IAEA for AI could audit labs and track compute without becoming a world government, and only needs the US and China. The US already pitched China an AI incident alert system in September
• A CERN for AI concentrates power, so if its AI went wrong, no other lab could build defenses
• The GPU-melting "Eliezer plan," which Altman reportedly called terrible, comes from Yudkowsky's 2022 "AGI Ruin" and its "pivotal act" to stop anyone else from building AGI
• John Schulman's counter is to deploy AI iteratively, raising the stakes a little each time and using each model to supervise the next

@theojaffee: "It was focused on building the first superintelligence and then using that superintelligence to perform a pivotal act to disempower everyone else in the world. Now, I think this is pretty bad. It eventually is equivalent to plotting to take over the world to usher in a utopia."

items.content:
Today is the first time a friend living in a small town in Austria with a regular software job in a regular traditional company finally got fully AI-pilled

He's in the group chat:

"It's crazy, everything takes me only 5 seconds now"

"This is the future guys"

"I don't care what he does as long as he's doing the work"

"My employer yesterday said we our CMS renews soon for a $10K/year license, so we'll cancel it and vibe code our own dashboard now lol"

"Being a coder in 2027 will only be about taste"

"Code is over"

Obviously on X all of us have already been using AI to code for years now and I haven't read code for over a year myself, but this is the first time I hear someone working not in a startup but a regular software job in a small town in Europe starts to say this kind of stuff

So maybe a signal AI coding has really reached mainstream? I thought it already did but apparently it didn't!

Attached a random location but kind of like his town (he asked to stay anon)

items.content:
this is great deepdive into what a managed harness looks like! some quick thoughts while reading:

- many diff types of agents built on it. doesnt surprise me - a lot of agents look very similar inside these days

- why not use off the shelf? (1) model and provider agnostic), (2) co-build with product teams, (3) own observability stack. I very much agree with points 1 and 3!!! and is something we obviously emphasize at langchain

- "The simplest agent harnesses are truly just a while loop, but when you want to support a wide array of agentic products in production, the responsibility of the harness or framework expands quite a bit" - +100 to this, is why were investing in deepagents so much

- "Using the “sandbox-as-a-tool” paradigm" - the massive trend seems to be going this way (is how deepagents is architected)

- "Supporting non-blocking async agents as the default". we are working on this right now for deepagents! agree is the future

- "The Connectors Service is the standard interface through which agents at Ramp interact with data sources. It centralizes authentication, credential management, access controls, and tool execution behind one API. This allows us to build and maintain integrations once, and reuse them across products." Also very important! and something we're thinking a bunch about for managed deepagents

items.content:
It worked

Of course it worked!

It never ever doesn't work right?

I vibecoded my own Spotify that works with Amazon Alexa and plays all my own MP3 music files 😊 

Claude Code calls it the 🎶 Jukebox

I put some coffee jazz MP3s (that I purchased) in an R2 bucket, made an Alexa skill in the Alexa Developer Console with help from Claude Code and now it plays it if I ask "Alexa, coffee jazz"

It wrote a package.json and index.js, then I saved and built it on the console. Then I had to manually add a Routine to Alexa so that "Alexa, coffee jazz" became "Alexa, ask the jukebox to play coffee jazz"

It also has Bossa Nova and Lofi and I can just drop music in whenever I want and it auto plays it

Spotify with Alexa was giving me really terrible recommendations of music and always the same and the only thing I used it for was this!

So I guess I can cancel Spotify now too 🙏

I vibecoded my own Spotify that works with Amazon Alexa and plays all my own MP3 music files 😊

Claude Code calls it the 🎶 Jukebox

I put some coffee jazz MP3s (that I purchased) in an R2 bucket, made an Alexa skill in the Alexa Developer Console with help from Claude Code and now it plays it if I ask "Alexa, coffee jazz"

It wrote a package.json and index.js, then I saved and built it on the console. Then I had to manually add a Routine to Alexa so that "Alexa, coffee jazz" became "Alexa, ask the jukebox to play coffee jazz"

It also has Bossa Nova and Lofi and I can just drop music in whenever I want and it auto plays it

Spotify with Alexa was giving me really terrible recommendations of music and always the same and the only thing I used it for was this!

So I guess I can cancel Spotify now too 🙏

items.title: Mistral has released new Speech models! Voxtral Small Transcribe 3 takes the #3 spot on the Artifici...
items.content:
Mistral has released new Speech models! Voxtral Small Transcribe 3 takes the #3 spot on the Artificial Analysis Speech to Text leaderboard, and Voxtral 3 TTS enters the top 12 in both Text to Speech arenas

@MistralAI has released Voxtral 3: a new Text to Speech model and three Speech to Text models (Small Transcribe 3, Mini Transcribe 3 and Mini Transcribe Realtime 3). We evaluated all of them.

Key takeaways:

➤ Speech to Text: Voxtral Small Transcribe 3 takes the #3 spot on the Artificial Analysis Speech to Text leaderboard with a 2.1% AA-WER Index, ahead of ElevenLabs Scribe v2 (2.2%) and Grok Voice Transcribe 2.0 (2.3%). Voxtral Mini Transcribe 3 lands at #5 with 2.2%.

➤ Streaming Speech to Text: Voxtral Mini Transcribe Realtime 3 scores 3.3% final-transcript AA-WER at the 960 ms setting (#6 of 46) and 3.6% at 480 ms, down from 5.2% for the previous Voxtral Mini Transcribe Realtime.

➤ Text to Speech, Provider Voice: Voxtral 3 TTS scores an Elo of 1,218 across 1,599 arena appearances, ranking #12 of 98, just behind Breeze TTS 2 at 1,221 and ahead of Inworld Realtime TTS-2 Flash and StepAudio 2.5 TTS at 1,216. It ranks #13 in English (US) and #12 in English (UK).

➤ Text to Speech, Controlled Voice: Voxtral 3 TTS scores 1,068 across 1,614 appearances, ranking #12 of 43 with the same 8 cloned voices, behind Eleven v3 at 1,072 and level with Ant Group's Ming-3.0-tts at 1,068. It ranks #10 in Assistants and #10 in English (UK).

➤ Pronunciation Robustness: Voxtral 3 TTS scores 84.4%, ranking #13 of 32 models, behind Qwen-Audio-3.1-TTS-Plus at 84.6% and ahead of HeyGen Voice at 83.2%. It ranks #3 in Standalone Terms at 93.9%.

➤ Pricing: Voxtral 3 TTS is priced at $13/1M characters, compared to Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS at $16.5/1M characters, Eleven v4 Turbo at $40/1M characters and Simba 3.2 at $6.6/1M characters.

See more details and listen to samples below ⬇️

items.content:
This will make language models generate text much faster.

Normally, a model generates one token at a time.

But with this tool, a smaller helper model guesses several upcoming tokens, and the main model checks those guesses together.

When the guesses are right, you get several tokens in one pass.

They made the code available, and you can run this with vLLM and SGLang.

Sophont CEO @iScienceLuvr reveals how Holon-S1 matched a medical team's findings from expensive molecular tests in a rare bone cancer case, using just a biopsy slide:

"We looked at a patient with a rare type of bone cancer called osteosarcoma. Our model wasn’t actually trained on osteosarcoma, but it was able to extract a lot of biological insights that this patient’s medical team had also observed. items.title: Once Intelligence Index thresholds are reached, the cost of accessing that level of intelligence red...
items.content:
Once Intelligence Index thresholds are reached, the cost of accessing that level of intelligence reduces fast. Reaching 30 on the Intelligence Index now costs 86x less per task than when first reached

Existing intelligence thresholds have become cheaper to reach, while the highest-scoring model costs more than the highest-scoring from one year ago.

Key takeaways:

➤ Reaching 20 is 123x cheaper than ~13 months ago; reaching 40 is 33x cheaper than ~5 months ago: measured models first reached these thresholds in September 2025 and May 2026.

➤ GPT-6 Luna (high) reaches 30 for $0.03/task: @OpenAI's model is 86x cheaper per task than @AnthropicAI's Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Adaptive Reasoning, Max Effort), which first reached 30 in February 2026 at $2.49/task.

➤ Claude Haiku 5.5 (xhigh) is now cheapest to reach 40: it scores 41 at $0.12/task, 5% below GPT-6.1 Sol (low).

➤ Reaching 50 is 18x cheaper than when first reached: GPT-6.1 Sol (high) reaches it for $0.32/task.

➤ The highest measured score has risen from 21 to 58 in a year, at ~11x the cost: Claude Opus 5.5 (Adaptive Reasoning, Max Effort, Default Fallback) costs $5.98/task.

As of October 20, 2026, using measured v4.3.2 results and current prices, including for historical models.

items.title: Fibo 2.0 from @bria_ai_ is the #1 open weights model on AA-Image-Editing v2.1 and statistically tied...
items.content:
Fibo 2.0 from @bria_ai_ is the #1 open weights model on AA-Image-Editing v2.1 and statistically tied with Qwen-Image-2.1 for the lead on AA-Image-T2I v2.1, a large step up from Bria's first-generation Fibo models on both leaderboards

Fibo 2.0 is Bria’s new 8B parameter open weights image model. The weights are released under a non-commercial license, which requires a separate agreement with Bria for commercial use. Bria released two sets of open weights: Fibo 2.0 Dev for Text to Image, and Fibo 2.0 Edit Turbo, a faster distilled model, for Image Editing. We benchmarked Fibo 2.0 through the Bria API at its default settings.

Fibo 2.0 is level with Qwen-Image-2.1 as the leading open weights model on both AA-Image-Editing v2.1 and AA-Image-T2I v2.1. It is a large step up from Bria's first-generation Fibo models on both leaderboards: it scores higher on every editing action and Text to Image capability we measure, with the biggest gains in Text or Symbol Edits, Text Rendering and Layout.

Fibo 2.0 costs $32 per 1k images on the Bria API. Luma UNI 1 Max ($100 per 1k images) and Qwen Image 2.0 Pro ($75) cost more and score slightly lower on both leaderboards, while Grok Imagine Image Quality scores about the same at $50. It is available through the Bria API and fal, with open weights on Hugging Face.

Congratulations to @bria_ai_ on the release!

See below for our analysis and example outputs of Fibo 2.0 on AA-Image-Editing v2.1 and AA-Image-T2I v2.1 🧵

items.content:
⚡️ Solid work from the Physis-AI Infra team. Together with Physis-AI, we’re introducing PhysisServe.

PhysisServe advances autoregressive denoising serving via fine-grained stage pipelining, time-sharing and multi-stream joint scheduling, optimizing both single-stream output latency and multi-stream system efficiency in one inference system.

PhysisServe’s core techniques are coming to vLLM-Omni, and our teams are working closely together to make it happen.

Congrats on a strong debut. Excited for what we’ll build together! 👏

items.title: Sophont CEO @iScienceLuvr explains how Holon-S1 can extract insights that usually require expensive ...
items.content:
Sophont CEO @iScienceLuvr explains how Holon-S1 can extract insights that usually require expensive molecular tests from an ordinary cancer biopsy slide:

"Why is it so hard to cure cancer? Because cancer’s a very diverse disease. Even though two people may have the same exact diagnosis, the underlying biology can be quite different."

"There are various tools for doing this, molecular tests and so on, but a lot of these tools can be quite expensive and time-consuming. Can we extract a lot of those similar insights directly from a tissue slide?"

"Whenever a cancer patient has a solid tumor, the gold standard is you take a biopsy, put it on a slide, under the microscope, and a doctor is analyzing that."

"We can take that same exact slide and with AI extract a lot more information about what’s happening at the molecular level, what genes are being expressed, and what makes that tumor unique for that patient."
@SophontAI

items.title:
Here is the prompt to build your own music MP3 player and internet radio for Amazon Alexa:

[ 🎶 Juke...
items.content:
Here is the prompt to build your own music MP3 player and internet radio for Amazon Alexa:

[ 🎶 Jukebox for Alexa ] by @levelsio 

Build me a private Alexa skill that plays my own music from a cloud bucket, plus internet radio

I want my Amazon Echo to play my own MP3s instead of being forced to use Amazon Music or Spotify. Build a private Alexa skill for this. Do as much as possible yourself: use CLIs and APIs, deploy and test it yourself, and only ask me for things only a person can do (logging in, clicking Allow, testing on the Echo).

Setup
- My music is in an S3-compatible bucket (AWS S3 or Cloudflare R2) under a music/ prefix. Each folder under it is a genre/playlist (music/Coffee Jazz/) or an artist/album (music/Artist/Album/).
- I'll create an access key for the bucket and give it to you. Keep it in a config file and never print it. The skill only needs read access; the upload tools need write access.
- My Echo and my Amazon developer account use the same Amazon login.

Build
1. An Alexa-hosted (Node.js) custom skill with invocation name "jukebox" (use two words if Amazon rejects one) and the AudioPlayer interface enabled.
2. Voice model: a PlayIntent with an AMAZON.SearchQuery slot ("play {query}", "put on {query}", "tune in to {query}", "shuffle {query}"), a ShuffleAllIntent, a WhatsPlayingIntent, a ListStationsIntent, and all the built-in AudioPlayer intents (pause, resume, next, previous, loop on/off, shuffle on/off, start over).
3. Library: list everything under music/ with ListObjectsV2 (follow the continuation token), build folders from the key prefixes, keep only .mp3/.m4a/.aac files, and cache the result for 5 minutes. Match spoken phrases to folder and file names loosely: ignore track numbers and spacing ("ama piano" = amapiano), turn number words into digits ("thirteen beaches" = 13 Beaches), and handle genre aliases (dnb, drum n bass, hiphop, lo fi).
4. Playback: give Alexa a presigned HTTPS GET URL for each file. Make it valid for at least 12 hours so long mixes and pause/resume don't expire mid-play. Keep the bucket private. Store the play queue in the AudioPlayer token (folder, shuffle seed, position) so there's no database, and enqueue the next track on PlaybackNearlyFinished. Folders shuffle and loop. A folder whose files all start with track numbers is an album and plays in order. A single song carries on with the rest of its folder.
5. Radio: a stations list of HTTPS MP3/AAC/HLS streams, with good underground electronic stations (Rinse FM, NTS, Bassdrive, Intergalactic FM, Kiosk Radio, Refuge Worldwide, and so on) plus news (BBC World Service, NPR). Test every URL with curl first and drop the plain-HTTP ones, because Alexa refuses them. Support "play rinse fm", "drum and bass radio", "techno radio" and "the news", and make next/previous switch stations. Live streams drop and Alexa treats a drop as the end, so re-enqueue the same stream with a new token on PlaybackNearlyFinished, and retry once on PlaybackFailed.

When it works, tell me how to add Alexa app routines (When: voice "coffee jazz" → Action: Customized "ask jukebox to play coffee jazz") so I can just say "Alexa, coffee jazz". And how to play internet radio stations I like.

Here is the prompt to build your own music MP3 player and internet radio for Amazon Alexa:

[ 🎶 Jukebox for Alexa ] by @levelsio

Build me a private Alexa skill that plays my own music from a cloud bucket, plus internet radio

I want my Amazon Echo to play my own MP3s instead of being forced to use Amazon Music or Spotify. Build a private Alexa skill for this. Do as much as possible yourself: use CLIs and APIs, deploy and test it yourself, and only ask me for things only a person can do (logging in, clicking Allow, testing on the Echo).

Setup

  • My music is in an S3-compatible bucket (AWS S3 or Cloudflare R2) under a music/ prefix. Each folder under it is a genre/playlist (music/Coffee Jazz/) or an artist/album (music/Artist/Album/).
  • I'll create an access key for the bucket and give it to you. Keep it in a config file and never print it. The skill only needs read access; the upload tools need write access.
  • My Echo and my Amazon developer account use the same Amazon login.

Build

1. An Alexa-hosted (Node.js) custom skill with invocation name "jukebox" (use two words if Amazon rejects one) and the AudioPlayer interface enabled.

2. Voice model: a PlayIntent with an AMAZON.SearchQuery slot ("play {query}", "put on {query}", "tune in to {query}", "shuffle {query}"), a ShuffleAllIntent, a WhatsPlayingIntent, a ListStationsIntent, and all the built-in AudioPlayer intents (pause, resume, next, previous, loop on/off, shuffle on/off, start over).

3. Library: list everything under music/ with ListObjectsV2 (follow the continuation token), build folders from the key prefixes, keep only .mp3/.m4a/.aac files, and cache the result for 5 minutes. Match spoken phrases to folder and file names loosely: ignore track numbers and spacing ("ama piano" = amapiano), turn number words into digits ("thirteen beaches" = 13 Beaches), and handle genre aliases (dnb, drum n bass, hiphop, lo fi).

4. Playback: give Alexa a presigned HTTPS GET URL for each file. Make it valid for at least 12 hours so long mixes and pause/resume don't expire mid-play. Keep the bucket private. Store the play queue in the AudioPlayer token (folder, shuffle seed, position) so there's no database, and enqueue the next track on PlaybackNearlyFinished. Folders shuffle and loop. A folder whose files all start with track numbers is an album and plays in order. A single song carries on with the rest of its folder.

5. Radio: a stations list of HTTPS MP3/AAC/HLS streams, with good underground electronic stations (Rinse FM, NTS, Bassdrive, Intergalactic FM, Kiosk Radio, Refuge Worldwide, and so on) plus news (BBC World Service, NPR). Test every URL with curl first and drop the plain-HTTP ones, because Alexa refuses them. Support "play rinse fm", "drum and bass radio", "techno radio" and "the news", and make next/previous switch stations. Live streams drop and Alexa treats a drop as the end, so re-enqueue the same stream with a new token on PlaybackNearlyFinished, and retry once on PlaybackFailed.

6. Log one line per request (type, intent, token, offset, error) so playback problems show up in CloudWatch.

  • Install the ASK CLI (npm i -g ask-cli). If ask configure won't work in your shell, run ask util generate-lwa-tokens --no-browser, have me paste the one-time code, and write ~/.ask/cli_config yourself. Get the vendor ID from GET https://t.co/8eS787CaBt.
  • The hosted skill's code is a git repo (find it with ask smapi get-alexa-hosted-skill-metadata). Push to master to deploy, with ask util git-credentials-helper as the git credential helper. The helper needs ask-resources.json and .ask/ask-states.json next to the repo. If pushes start failing with 403, clear the cached macOS keychain credential.

items.content:
When you send a prompt to a model, a couple of things happen:

1. The model processes the prompt and generates the first token (prefill stage).

2. Then, the model continuously processes the prompt + new tokens until it produces the complete answer (decode stage)

These guys are doing something really cool:

They are using different hardware for each stage. They run prefill on GPUs and decode on Positron's specialized inference systems.

This results in faster generation.

items.content:

items.title: Sophont CEO @iScienceLuvr explains the cognitive dissonance of frontier AI labs promising cancer bre...
items.content:
Sophont CEO @iScienceLuvr explains the cognitive dissonance of frontier AI labs promising cancer breakthroughs a decade away when AI could help patients right now:

"Anthropic is releasing various blog posts and interesting projects, but it’s still very limited in scope. I think it’s a very promising direction. The challenge is that the timelines are gonna be very long."

"If we’re telling people AI can save lives and cure cancer, but people are waiting 10 years, it’s very hard for people to understand. There are interesting things that can actually have impact right now."

"The labs are all promising they’re gonna have all this impact, but it’s gonna take a while. There’s a little bit of cognitive dissonance going on that people are now starting to catch on to."
@SophontAI

items.content:
Kong CTO @subnetmarco predicts the shift from engineers coding until 4 AM to watching AI agents do the work is coming for every department:

"We’re not going to be the unit of compute anymore as humans. We’re going to be the architects of agentic loops where the agents do the work for us."

"Many engineers used to write code until 4:00 AM chasing a bug. Today they’re just looking at the screen, looking at their agents doing the work for them. That same change is coming to legal, HR, IT, security, customer success, sales."

"I’m not saying we’re replacing humans. Humans will change. But the work itself is not going to be done by us anymore. Everything has to be an event, and we create agents that react to those events."
@kong

items.title: Coco Labs CEO @anurahk, who helped launch Google's first image and video models, reveals the AI same...
items.content:
Coco Labs CEO @anurahk, who helped launch Google's first image and video models, reveals the AI sameness problem that made her quit to build a model for taste:

"I was previously working on launching the very first image and video generation models at Google, in Brain and DeepMind, and that’s when I noticed this particular problem that all models converge to the average."

"We call it the AI average or the AI sameness. The purple gradient, the purple premium that people talk about a lot."

"I got thinking a couple of years ago on how can we actually solve taste, because taste is the biggest problem in design. That motivated me and David, my co-founder, to quit and start Coco Labs."

"Vyb tries to understand the user’s taste. The artistic direction, what fonts, what typography, imagery, graphics. What does the user lean towards? Because it’s anchored in the user’s taste, the design gears away from being AI average."
@cocoailabs

Oh. My. God. 

I just called Michaels.

@instinct @noahrshinn explain - is it a human or an AI?

items.title: Krea 3 Ultra comes closest to the frontier on Reasoning-Based Edits, where it ranks #4 and Krea 3 Fa...
items.content:
Krea 3 Ultra comes closest to the frontier on Reasoning-Based Edits, where it ranks #4 and Krea 3 Fast ranks #20

Our Image Arena taxonomy measures 7 editing actions and 10 use cases for Image Editing. Editing actions measure what an edit asks the model to do.

Krea 3 Ultra ranks in the top 7 on 6 of the 7 editing actions, with its best rank on Composition & Framing (#3). Reasoning-Based Edits show the largest difference between the two modes. Its lowest-ranked action is Scene & Style Edit (#17), where Krea 3 Fast ranks #11.

➤ Reasoning-Based Edit covers edits that need inference about the scene rather than a literal instruction.

➤ Composition & Framing covers cropping, extending, reframing, and changes to camera view or perspective.

➤ Scene & Style Edit covers relighting, restyling, and changes to the background, setting or overall treatment.

items.title: Krea 3 Ultra lands at #5 on AA-Image-Editing v2.1, with quality similar to Nano Banana 2.1 and MAI-I...
items.content:
Krea 3 Ultra lands at #5 on AA-Image-Editing v2.1, with quality similar to Nano Banana 2.1 and MAI-Image-2.6

Krea 3, released on October 15, is Krea's new image editing model and its first on our Image Editing leaderboard. Today Krea adds Ultra, its highest thinking mode, alongside the default Fast mode, and we tested both modes through the Krea API at 2K resolution.

Krea 3 Ultra is the highest-ranked image editing model from outside OpenAI, Google and Microsoft. It places in the top 7 in 15 of our 17 Image Editing categories. Its best results are in Animation & Gaming and Frontier, at #2 in both. Krea 3 Fast, the default mode, lands at #11.

On the Krea API, Krea 3 Fast costs $0.03 per 1K image, plus $0.02 per 1K reference image. Krea 3 Ultra supports 2K output only, and costs $0.27 for a 2K edit with one 1K reference image.

Krea 3 is available on Krea's API and through other 3rd party APIs.

Congratulations to @krea_ai on the release!

See below for our analysis and example outputs of Krea 3 in the Artificial Analysis Image Arena 🧵

items.title:
🇵🇱 Okay my final Poland video because we're leaving soon!

It was really fun and we had a great time...
items.content:
🇵🇱 Okay my final Poland video because we're leaving soon!

It was really fun and we had a great time

I liked Warsaw most to be honest, a very modern city, a bit like East Asia in terms of modernity, with rapid delivery services and apps, everything just works great and fast

I'm not saying it's perfect btw, there's moments where you still realize it's Eastern Europe (or as they'd like to call it Central Europe) but then the difference is they generally solve problems fast and pragmatically

Many shops you go will actually have a long line at the checkout, annoying, but usually there's a second checkout but it's closed

That's because Poland too has a big labor shortage, one of the lowest fertility rates in Europe, so they too kinda have to import people, but they choose to import them from Ukraine and Belarus (and some South Asians actually too)

But wait, so that checkout line is closed yes? I'm so used to Portugal where there is zero incentive to then open another checkout counter but in Poland usually within a few minutes they notice it's busy and open another counter. I know, basic stuff but hard to come by these days. They're fast and pragmatic

Ordering flowers for my gf was easy, the flower shop has an IG (but I don't) so I msg them over Whatsapp, they immediately respond, give me some options, I say what I want, address, payment link with Stripe (!) and done delivered at my hotel by a nice guy. All soooo smooth. Fast response, friendly people. Things just work here!

Poland has done a great job keeping bad immigrants out while bring good immigrants in. The Ukrainians and Belarussians are neighbors and their cultures overlap strongly with Poland. So they fit in easily. Same cultures, same religions, same routines etc. for the most part

A young Polish Uber driver I talked to said to him Krakow (his city) looks just like Lviv in Ukraine, so it's easy for Ukranians in Poland to integrate

There's a lot of police presence in places, and military vehicles also (probably cause of the Ukraine war), the security at the Warsaw Airport is not done by some 5 layer outsourced company with staff that hates you, but by friendly people from the Polish Border Guard (Straż Graniczna) wearing military uniforms

Warsaw has lots of skyscrapers now, and actually the tallest in Europe now at 310 meters is the Varso Tower, crazy!

Poland is a booming economy and growing fast. When you're growing of course it's easy to make things go well. I'd say it's important for Poland to look ahead carefully and don't make the same mistakes that Western Europe did when everything was going well and we were very rich

We became complacent, stagnant, added regulatory burdens, became overly obsessed with climate change and the environment, and imported the lowest quality tier of people from cultures that hate our guys and are diametrically opposed to Western culture

That last part is especially interesting considering Poland's history, where 6 million (!) or 20% of the country was ruthlessly murdered in World War II

I think that gives them the power to not have to be politically correct about immigration like Germany, because Poland after all was the victim, while Germany then was the purpetreyor. Which is why Germany does have to be so politically correct about it, due to extreme historical guilt

You walk on the streets of Poland in the day and at night and you see the difference what sane policy does to daily life

We're all dealing with the echoes of history

So my message to my Polish friends: don't make the same mistakes Western Europe did and you will soon be the richest, safest, most modern country in Europe and hopefully then have the power to be the new leader of Europe

And maybe you can then save Europe as a whole!!

Niech żyje Polska! 🇵🇱

➤ Standalone Terms: 93.9%, ranking #3 behind Fish Audio Drama 3 Preview at 95.9% and Eleven v3 Conversational at 95.1%

➤ Contextually Appropriate: 91.9%, with Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS leading at 97.9%

➤ Expanding Shorthand: 80.2%, level with Qwen-Audio-3.1-TTS-Plus at 80.2%, with Ming-3.0-tts leading at 96.5%

➤ Preserving Exact Sequences: 75.5%, with Ming-3.0-tts leading at 90.6%

To be released soon by @PacktPublishing

“Claude is powerful, but many people use it in fragile, one-off ways. You prompt, get an answer, and move on. Real work, however, is not a single prompt; it is a sequence of tasks, decisions, and context.

This book shows you how to move from prompts to skills and toward true agentic engineering. Instead of refining prompts, you will learn a practical, structured way of working with AI by designing skills and workflows that produce consistent results and can be tested, improved, and reused.

Rather than teaching you to rely on tools that quickly become outdated, this book helps build a durable mental model for working with AI. By the end, you will not just prompt AI but design how work is carried out with it, using Claude or any AI tool of your choice.”
